'''Léon-Yves Bottou<ref name=":22">{{cite book |last1=LeCun |first1=Y. |title=Connectionism in Perspective: Proceedings of the International Conference Connectionism in Perspective, University of Zurich, 10–13 October 1988 |date=1989 |publisher=Elsevier |editor-last1=Pfeifer |editor-first1=R. |location=Amsterdam |chapter=Generalization and network design strategies |editor-last2=Schreter |editor-first2=Z. |editor-last3=Fogelman |editor-first3=F. |editor-last4=Steels |editor-first4=L. |chapter-url=https://masters.donntu.ru/2012/fknt/umiarov/library/lecun.pdf}}</ref>''' ({{IPA|fr|leɔ̃ bɔtu}}; born 1965) is a researcher best known for his work in [[machine learning]] and [[data compression]]. His work presents [[stochastic gradient descent]] as a fundamental learning algorithm.<ref name="stochastic_research">{{cite web |last1=Bottou |first1=Léon |title=Learning with Stochastic Gradient Descent |url=https://leon.bottou.org/research/stochastic |website=leon.bottou.org |access-date=14 May 2024}}</ref> He is also one of the main creators of the [[DjVu]] image compression technology (together with [[Yann LeCun]] and Patrick Haffner), and the maintainer of [https://djvu.sf.net DjVuLibre], the open source implementation of DjVu. He is the original developer of the [[Lush (programming language)|Lush]] programming language.

==Life==
Léon Bottou was born in France in 1965. He obtained the [[Diplôme d'Ingénieur]] from [[École Polytechnique]] in 1987, a Magistère de Mathématiques Fondamentales et Appliquées et d’Informatique from [[École Normale Supérieure]] in 1988, a Diplôme d'Études Approndies in Computer Science in 1988, in 1988, and a PhD from [[Université Paris-Sud]] in 1991.<ref>{{Cite web |title=biography [leon.bottou.org] |url=https://leon.bottou.org/biography |access-date=2025-05-24 |website=leon.bottou.org}}</ref>

In 1988, in collaboration with [[Yann LeCun]], he published SN, a software package for simulating artificial neural networks.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bottou |first=Leon |last2=Lecun |first2=Yann |date=1988 |title=SN : Un simulateur pour réseaux connexionnistes |trans-title=Sn: A simulator for connectionist models |url=https://atcold.github.io/2024/08/05/SN.html |journal=Proceedings of NeuroNimes 88, Nimes, France}}</ref> His master's thesis<ref>Bottou, Léon-Yves (1988) Master's thesis. École des Hautes Études en Informatique (EHEI) at Université de Paris 5.</ref> concerned using [[Time delay neural network|Time Delay Neural Networks]] for [[speech recognition]].<ref name=":2">{{cite book |last1=LeCun |first1=Y. |title=Connectionism in Perspective: Proceedings of the International Conference Connectionism in Perspective, University of Zurich, 10–13 October 1988 |date=1989 |publisher=Elsevier |editor-last1=Pfeifer |editor-first1=R. |location=Amsterdam |chapter=Generalization and network design strategies |editor-last2=Schreter |editor-first2=Z. |editor-last3=Fogelman |editor-first3=F. |editor-last4=Steels |editor-first4=L. |chapter-url=https://masters.donntu.ru/2012/fknt/umiarov/library/lecun.pdf}}</ref> He then joined the Adaptive Systems Research Department at [[AT&T]] [[Bell Laboratories]] in [[Holmdel, New Jersey]], where he collaborated with [[Vladimir Vapnik]] on local learning algorithms.<ref>{{cite journal |first1=Vladimir N. |last1=Vapnik |first2=Léon |last2=Bottou |title=Local Algorithms for Pattern Recognition and Dependencies Estimation |journal=Neural Computation |volume=5 |issue=6 |pages=893–909 |year=1993 |doi=10.1162/neco.1993.5.6.893 |s2cid=2327934 }}</ref>

in 1992, he returned to France and founded Neuristique S.A., a company that produced machine learning tools and one of the first data mining software packages, including Lush, an object-oriented programming language based on [[C (programming language)|C]] and [[Lisp (programming language)|Lisp]] designed for training and using large-scale neural networks.<ref>{{Cite web |title=projects:lush [leon.bottou.org] |url=https://leon.bottou.org/projects/lush |access-date=2025-08-15 |website=leon.bottou.org}}</ref> In 1995, he returned to Bell Laboratories, where he developed a number of new machine learning methods, such as Graph Transformer Networks (similar to [[conditional random field]]), and applied them to handwriting recognition and OCR.<ref>{{cite journal |first1=Yann |last1=LeCun |first2=Léon |last2=Bottou |first3=Yoshua |last3=Bengio |first4=Patrick |last4=Haffner |title=Gradient Based Learning Applied to Document Recognition |journal=[[Proceedings of the IEEE]] |volume=86 |issue=11 |pages=2278–2324 |year=1998 |doi=10.1109/5.726791 |s2cid=14542261 |url=https://elartu.tntu.edu.ua/handle/lib/38369 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> The bank check recognition system that he helped develop was widely deployed by NCR and other companies, reading over 10% of all the checks in the US in the late 1990s and early 2000s.

In 1996, he joined [[AT&T Labs]] and worked primarily on the [[DjVu]] image compression technology,<ref>{{cite journal |first1=Léon |last1=Bottou |first2=Patrick |last2=Haffner |first3=Paul G. |last3=Howard |first4=Patrice |last4=Simard |first5=Yoshua |last5=Bengio |first6=Yann |last6=LeCun |display-authors=1 |title=High Quality Document Image Compression with DjVu |journal=[[Journal of Electronic Imaging]] |volume=7 |issue=3 |pages=410–425 |year=1998 |doi=10.1117/1.482609 |bibcode=1998JEI.....7..410B |citeseerx=10.1.1.38.4518 }}</ref> that is used by some websites, notably the [[Internet Archive]], to distribute scanned documents. Between 2002 and 2010, he was a research scientist at NEC Laboratories in [[Princeton, New Jersey]], where he focused on the theory and practice of machine learning with large-scale datasets,<ref>{{cite book |title=Large Scale Kernel Machines |editor-first=Léon |editor-last=Bottou |editor2-first=Olivier |editor2-last=Chapelle |editor3-first=Dennis |editor3-last=DeCoste |editor4-first=Jason |editor4-last=Weston |series=Neural Information Processing Series |publisher=MIT Press |location=Cambridge, MA |year=2007 |isbn=978-0-262-02625-3 }}</ref> on-line learning, and stochastic optimization methods.<ref>{{cite book |first=Léon |last=Bottou |chapter=Stochastic Learning |title=Advanced Lectures on Machine Learning |pages=146–168 |editor-first=Olivier |editor-last=Bousquet |editor2-first=Ulrike |editor2-last=von Luxburg |series=Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence |volume=3176 |publisher=Springer Verlag |location=Berlin |year=2004 |isbn=978-3-540-23122-6 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=60CAolt0cpgC&pg=PA146 }}</ref> He developed the open source software [[LaSVM]] for fast large-scale [[support vector machine]], and [[stochastic gradient descent]] software for training linear SVM and Conditional Random Fields. In 2010 he joined the Microsoft adCenter in [[Redmond, Washington]], and in 2012 became a Principal Researcher at [[Microsoft Research]] in New York City. In March 2015 he joined [[Meta AI|Facebook Artificial Intelligence Research]], also in New York City, as a research lead.

His work in gradient descent argued that both stochastic gradient descent and batch gradient descent reach similar levels of loss with the same number of training samples, but SGD is faster when running on large datasets. He also argued that second-order gradient descent methods, such as [[Quasi-Newton method|quasi-Newton methods]], can be beneficial compared to plain SGD. See (Bottou et al 2018)<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bottou |first1=Léon |last2=Curtis |first2=Frank E. |last3=Nocedal |first3=Jorge |date=January 2018 |title=Optimization Methods for Large-Scale Machine Learning |url=https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/16M1080173 |journal=SIAM Review |language=en |volume=60 |issue=2 |pages=223–311 |doi=10.1137/16M1080173 |arxiv=1606.04838 |osti=1541717 |issn=0036-1445}}</ref> for a review.

He was program chair of the 2013 [[Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems]] and the 2009 [[International Conference on Machine Learning]]. In 2007, he was received one of the first [[Blavatnik Awards for Young Scientists]] from the [[Blavatnik Family Foundation]] and the [[New York Academy of Sciences]].
